name: Late Payment Regulation
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: impact assessment forecasts with clear targets; contested by stakeholders; not adopted
summary: The Commission set a clear target - cutting the share of firms reporting late payment as a problem from 43% to 28% - and expected a strict 30-day payment limit to shorten payment times by about 35%. Business groups and trade credit insurers dispute the costs, and the proposal has stalled in the Council, so none of these promises can yet be tested.

indicators.indicator: Share of companies reporting late payments as a problem (ECB/Commission SAFE survey)
indicators.evidence: Not applicable: regulation not adopted (Parliament position 2024; blocking minority reported in Council).

indicators.objective: Fewer late payments, by firm size
indicators.indicator: Same SAFE indicator per size class
Payment times cut ~35%; hassle costs of chasing debtors (340.2m hours, EUR 8.74bn) significantly reduced; EUR 27m/yr court savings from mediation
indicators.target_or_baseline: Costs: EUR 243m one-off (invoices); EUR 70-105m/yr public enforcement and mediation
indicators.evidence: Forecast only; industry (trade credit insurers) claims a strict 30-day cap creates up to EUR 2tn new financing need.

literature.citation: European Commission (2023), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on combating late payment in commercial transactions, SWD(2023) 314 (executive summary SWD(2023) 313)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on combating late payment in commercial transactions
literature.outcomes: payment times; administrative burden; SME cash flow
literature.headline: Payment times reduced by an estimated 35%; hassle costs of chasing debtors (340.2m hours, EUR 8.74bn) significantly reduced; mediation saves EUR 27m a year in court cases; one-off costs EUR 243m; public enforcement and mediation EUR 70-105m a year; ~41% of SMEs benefit from 30-day cap
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected a hard 30-day payment limit to shorten payment times by about 35% and save firms much of the EUR 8.7 billion a year they spend chasing late payers, at one-off costs of about EUR 243 million.

literature.citation: European Economic and Social Committee (2024), Opinion on the revision of the Late Payments Directive, EESC opinion INT/1041, adopted 17 January 2024
literature.title: Opinion on the revision of the Late Payments Directive
literature.headline: Strong concerns that the 30-day cap for business-to-business payments eliminates contractual freedom; welcomes 30 days for public authorities paying businesses; sees potential benefit in national enforcement bodies
literature.summary_plain: The EU's advisory committee of employers, unions and civil society backed a 30-day limit for public bodies but found a strict 30-day cap between businesses too rigid.

literature.citation: International Credit Insurance & Surety Association (ICISA) (2024), EU Late Payment Regulation: Blocking majority forms in European Council, ICISA news, 6 June 2024
literature.title: EU Late Payment Regulation: Blocking majority forms in European Council
literature.headline: Claims a strict 30-day term for B2B transactions would create a new financing requirement of up to EUR 2tn; reports a blocking majority forming in Council
literature.summary_plain: Trade credit insurers argue the 30-day cap would force firms to find up to EUR 2 trillion in extra financing; the figure is the industry's own and unverified.
literature.interested_party: Trade credit insurers' association whose business depends on payment terms
